text: You've made a strong case, and while I’m still skeptical about the specific chain of command, I’m leaning more toward Iroh having a higher level of culpability than I previously thought. I still view some actions as "wrongdoings" that fall short of war crimes. Sieges, colonization, and population displacement are brutal, but historically, they aren't always classified as war crimes—similar to the population replacement in Königsberg after WWII. These are the "standard" horrors of total war. The Rough Rhinos are the real issue. In a centralized autocracy like the Fire Nation, the chain of command likely bypassed the High General for "black-ops" or "high-value" units. If the Rhinos were the Fire Lord’s personal hounds (similar to a Wagner Group), a General—even a Prince—would have to play nice with them to avoid political suicide. Calling them "old friends" might not be an endorsement, but the weary diplomacy of an officer dealing with a unit that is "untouchable" by regular military law. The fact that they speak as peers ("Iroh," "Old Friend") suggests a history that exists outside the official chain of command. It implies they were either so close in the field that rank became irrelevant—which suggests deep complicity—or they belonged to different branches of the power structure and knew each other as fellow high-level assets. To "convict" Iroh, you’d need to prove he was an enabler with the power to act. If they were under his direct command, he is absolutely tied to those atrocities. text: The thing is though Iroh never really went through any great trials or struggle for redemption in the show. By the time we see him he’s essentially already finished 90% of his redemption arc and all that’s left is for him to atone for his actions, which he does in the series finale without hesitation or character development. Hell, he never even expresses guilt for his past actions outside of his son’s death and the only time anyone calls him out for his past is a no name earth kingdom soldier whose framed as unsympathetic and antagonistic. That’s why there’s such a disconnect and why people constantly bring him up in relation to Azula. We only ever see Iroh post the majority of his redemption arc and are only ever vaguely told about what he needs to redeem himself for, while with Azula we are only shown her while she is still young and has yet to reach the point to want to redeem herself. So it’s really easy to accept Iroh’s redemption at face value when we don’t ever see him being evil, while it’s really easy to not accept the possibility of Azula ever being able to redeem herself when we have only ever seen her when she’s evil. But logically speaking if it’s possible for Iroh to eventually find redemption after spending decades committing atrocities and leading the Fire Nation on the frontlines, then it should also be possible for Azula to eventually recognize the error of her ways and begin the path towards redemption.

text: The issue here is a misinterpretation of Iroh’s role. From the story’s point of view, Iroh is not framed as a criminal, and that’s completely fine. Avatar: The Last Airbender - TV show - never presents him as someone committing war crimes, and forcing that label onto him is importing a framework the narrative itself doesn’t support. But that doesn’t make what he was part of “right.” He was still a general in an unjust war. He still served a regime built on conquest. That’s morally problematic, even if it’s not framed in legal terms. And that distinction matters. You don’t need Iroh to be a criminal for his past to be wrong. In fact, making him a “war criminal” actually simplifies the character too much. The more interesting point is that he was a loyal, disciplined product of that system—someone who did what was expected of him—and later realized the system itself was wrong. Also, part of the confusion comes from people importing real-world political lenses directly into the discussion. You see this especially when even acknowledging something like “a siege can be lawful depending on how it’s conducted” becomes controversial—not because of the show, but because it clashes with someone’s real-world narrative about ongoing conflicts. That kind of bleed-over muddies the analysis. If someone can’t separate “what the story is saying” from “what I want this to mean in real life,” they end up forcing labels that don’t actually fit the character. If someone can’t see the problem in fighting for an unjust war unless it’s labeled a crime, then the issue isn’t with the character—it’s with how they’re evaluating it. Iroh’s arc isn’t about escaping punishment. It’s about recognizing that being a “good soldier” in a bad system is still something worth questioning—and, ultimately, something worth changing.

text: I think it's absolutely fine to analyse a story beyond how the work itself presents the story. The presentation and focus of a work shouldn't stop us from having a look at what lies beyond. Approaching a story by only looking at what it presents is a valid approach for an analysis. It's also valid to analyse how this is presented, and what is probably left out. That's not muddying the analysis, it's just two different but equally valid ways to look at the work and the story it tells. In the case of Avatar The Last Airbender, it's bound to be quite a gab between these two approaches because it's a cartoon for children while the main storyline inlcudes a 100 long war. It's only natural that discussions arise. It's absolutely fine to not take that second approach, and remain within the boundaries set by the story. Personally, I'm also not always up to a critical analysis of every story all the time. But critical analysis of how a work is presented, or critical interpretations based on conflicting ideas in the story shouldn't be labeled as a "misunderstanding" nor as a "muddied analysis" just because the story or story element wasn't intended to be scene that way. That kind of analysis has its own worth and justification to exist. Just as an example from a completely different topic: both in the movies and the books of Twilight, there are several instances of the Edward watching Bella sleep without her knowledge. Overall the book portrays this as romantic, because well, it's a romance between a vampire and a human. Yet many people have labeled that as "creepy" – and surely, that's also based on our own world view of the matter. It's a matter of perspective, but we relate to all stories based on our own experiences. That's just how it is: our experiences, thoughts and feelings shape our opinions on things. Now I wonder: just because a romance novel didn't intend this to come across as creepy, would it also muddy the analysis if readers/viewers label it as creepy in their interpretation of the character, while also acknowledging that it probably wasn't intended to come across like that?
